beats.narration: Begin by framing Introduction to Cryptographic Standards as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Consider this worked case: The NIST FIPS 180-4 standard specifies AES-256 as an approved algorithm for encryption. On screen, display a table comparing AES-128, AES-256, and ChaCha20 with their approved parameter sets. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis. Then summarize what the example demonstrates, what it does not establish, and what evidence would be needed next.
beats.title: Introduction to Cryptographic Standards
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a table comparing AES-128, AES-256, and ChaCha20 with their approved parameter sets.

beats.narration: Now define Encryption and Confidentiality precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Consider this worked case: Using AES in CBC mode with a 256-bit key ensures that plaintext data remains unreadable without the decryption key. On screen, show a flowchart illustrating key generation, encryption process, and decryption process with labeled security checks. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Encryption and Confidentiality
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a flowchart illustrating key generation, encryption process, and decryption process with labeled security checks.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Message Authentication and Digital Signatures operates in a concrete sequence. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Consider this worked case: A digital signature uses a private key to sign a message, while a message authentication code uses a shared secret to verify integrity. On screen, create a side-by-side diagram showing how a digital signature verifies sender authenticity versus how HMAC verifies message integrity. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Message Authentication and Digital Signatures
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Create a side-by-side diagram showing how a digital signature verifies sender authenticity versus how HMAC verifies message integrity.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Random Number Generation and make the decision criteria explicit. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Consider this worked case: Cryptographically secure random number generators produce unpredictable values for session keys and nonces to prevent replay attacks. On screen, illustrate a sequence of random numbers generated by a CSPRNG versus a pseudo-random number generator, highlighting unpredictability. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Random Number Generation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a sequence of random numbers generated by a CSPRNG versus a pseudo-random number generator, highlighting unpredictability.

beats.narration: Apply Key Management Practices to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Consider this worked case: A key management system automatically rotates encryption keys every 90 days and securely destroys old keys from memory and storage. On screen, draw a lifecycle diagram showing each stage of key management with icons for generation, distribution, storage, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Key Management Practices
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Draw a lifecycle diagram showing each stage of key management with icons for generation, distribution, storage, rotation, revocation, and destruction.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Modes of Operation, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Consider this worked case: In GCM mode, the encryption primitive processes data in blocks while simultaneously computing an authentication tag for integrity. On screen, show a block diagram of a cipher operating in GCM mode, highlighting block processing and authentication tag generation. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Modes of Operation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a block diagram of a cipher operating in GCM mode, highlighting block processing and authentication tag generation.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Implementation Validation with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Consider this worked case: FIPS validation ensures that a software implementation of AES matches the mathematical specifications and passes test vectors. On screen, display a checklist of validation criteria including test vectors, side-channel resistance, and compliance with FIPS requirements. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Implementation Validation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a checklist of validation criteria including test vectors, side-channel resistance, and compliance with FIPS requirements.

beats.narration: Use Secure Software Development Framework to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Consider this worked case: The SSDF framework organizes security practices into Prepare, Protect, Produce, and Respond groups to guide secure development. On screen, create a four-quadrant matrix labeled Prepare, Protect, Produce, and Respond, with each quadrant containing key practices. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Secure Software Development Framework
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Create a four-quadrant matrix labeled Prepare, Protect, Produce, and Respond, with each quadrant containing key practices.

beats.narration: Connect Prepare the Organization to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Consider this worked case: Training developers in secure coding standards and providing access to secure development tools establishes the foundation for secure practices. On screen, show a flowchart connecting people training, process documentation, and technology provisioning to secure development readiness. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Prepare the Organization
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a flowchart connecting people training, process documentation, and technology provisioning to secure development readiness.

beats.narration: Finish with Protect the Software as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Consider this worked case: Access control policies and code repository permissions ensure that only authorized developers can view or modify source code. On screen, illustrate a network diagram showing code repositories, access controls, and authentication mechanisms protecting development artifacts. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Protect the Software
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a network diagram showing code repositories, access controls, and authentication mechanisms protecting development artifacts.

sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.excerpt: A fast paced, informal look at current trends in the theory of computing. Each week is dedicated to a different topic and will explore some of the underlying theory as well as the practical applications of the theory. Sample topics may include: quantum cryptography, networks and complex systems, social welfare and game theory, zero knowledge protocols. Students will be evaluated on homework assignments and a final presentation. Offered every other year. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall
sources.title: RIT CSCI-464 Xtreme Theory catalog description

sources.author: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.excerpt: The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.
sources.title: NIST Secure Software Development Framework

Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.
